narrative:
Your law school application was not denied because of who you are, but because the model sees a very high likelihood that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. It placed that probability at 97%, meaning nearly certain failure based on the academic signals in your file.

The strongest signal was your third-year class ranking. You placed in the very bottom tenth of your class, while students who are typically accepted sit close to the middle of their class, around the sixth decile. Being so far at the bottom in your final year tells the model that you are struggling with the level of material required for success. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 23.5, far below the average of about 37 among accepted applicants. This matters because the LSAT measures the kind of reasoning skills the bar exam demands. A score that low makes it very hard to see you catching up. The third influential factor was your first-year class ranking, also in the bottom tenth, again far below the accepted average around the sixth decile. Together, these three factors all pushed the model strongly toward predicting bar exam failure.

The message is not that you can never succeed, but that the evidence from your academic performance and standardized test scores is not yet strong enough to justify admission. Your next step should be to address those weaknesses directly: consider retaking the LSAT after focused preparation, and if possible, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework that demonstrates mastery of demanding material. Improving in these areas would give any future application a much stronger foundation.
